Ten Perfections · Chapter 2

Baths. Some people love a warm bath, or a cold one (p. 16–30)

Pages 16–30 (15 pages)
Ten Perfections Baths. Some people love a warm bath, or a cold one (p. 16–30) p. 16

Baths. Some people love a warm bath, or a cold one, even when the body does not need it. The bath is fine. The clinging to the temperature is the thing to notice.

Letting go is happiness. An ancient text, the Cūḷaniddesa (a book of the Tipiṭaka), says that nekkhamma (letting go) is a refuge, a protection and a place of no danger, and that it comes with happiness. Only paññā (wisdom) sees this, by comparing the two ways of living and finding out which one is really better.

The sick man and the string. A sick man cannot turn over by himself. The nurse ties a string to the bed so he can pull himself round. Pulling the string gives the body a little comfort, but it gives the mind no ease at all. Beings burning with the kilesa (defilements16) are like that. They cannot pull themselves out by the comfort of a quiet life alone. They need the perfections17.

The story of Susīma. The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) thought that in his life as Susīma. Susīma was the son of the king’s priest, and he grew up with the prince. When the prince became king, he made Susīma his adviser. One day the king’s mother saw Susīma riding behind the king on an elephant, fell in love with him, and was so unhappy that she stopped eating. The king solved it by making Susīma the king, with his mother as queen, while he himself became the second in command.

Susīma now had a queen, a palace and a whole kingdom. And from that day he was weary of it all. The queen tried every trick to make him enjoy his reign18. Instead Susīma taught the court about both the delight and the misery of sense pleasures, and then he handed the kingdom back. He went to the forest, became an ascetic, and developed jhāna (deep calm of mind). The Buddha said that the queen was Rāhula’s mother, the king was Ānanda, and Susīma was himself.

Nobody can order it. Nobody can tell another person to stop clinging. Nobody can even order themselves to stop. What can happen is this: paññā (wisdom) comes to see that the clinging is not worth keeping. Then it begins, slowly, to let go.

Chapter 4. Paññā (wisdom)

“when the sun rose higher all the dewdrops that were hanging there disintegrated and disappeared”

Paññā (wisdom) is the cetasika (mental factor1) that understands things as they really are. Without it, none of the other perfections2 can do their full work. A person may be generous3, well behaved and patient, but the kilesa (defilements4) can never be removed unless paññā (wisdom) grows sharp enough to see the truth. The commentary5 gives three pictures for it.

Paññā (wisdom) What it is seeing straight into the true nature of things, like an arrow shot by a skilled archer What it does lights things up, like a lamp How it shows no confusion, like a good guide in a forest itself What it needs samādhi (a steady mind) or the four noble truths

The lamp. A man carries an oil lamp into a dark house. The darkness goes, and things can be seen. In the same way, when paññā (wisdom) arises6, the darkness of avijjā (ignorance7) goes and the four noble truths can be seen. The ancient texts say that paññā (wisdom) means “it penetrates”: it goes right through to the truth that “this is dukkha” (suffering8).

Prince Yudañjaya and the dewdrops. The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was once Yudañjaya, the king’s eldest son. Every day he gave mahā-dāna (a great offering of gifts). One morning, early, he went to the royal park. Dewdrops hung like strings of pearls on the tree tops, on the tips of the grass and on spiders’ webs. Then the sun rose, and one by one the dewdrops vanished.

the sun rises

dewdrops on a spider's web Like the dewdrops, all conditioned things arise and then disappear. dewdrops on the grass tips “These dewdrops came into being and then disappeared. Evenso are conditioned realities, the lives of all beings”

The prince thought: these dewdrops came and went. All things that arise because of conditions9, including the lives of every living being10, are like dewdrops on the grass. A great sense of saṃvega (urgency11) came over him. He asked his parents’ leave and went to the forest to live as an ascetic12.

Many people see dewdrops. Very few are stirred by them to compare their own lives with a dewdrop. When that kind of understanding arises, it should not be let slip. It should be thought about, so that it arises again and again. The commentary shows that in this one life the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) fulfilled all ten perfections: giving by his great offerings, letting go by leaving home, wisdom by his thought about the dewdrops, and the rest.

Old Piṅgiya. The brahmin13 (priest) Piṅgiya was a hundred and twenty years old. He was weak, and his eyes and ears were failing. He came to the Buddha and asked for only one thing: that the Buddha explain the teaching that makes an end of birth and old age. The Buddha told him that clinging14 to rūpa (matter15, the body and the things sensed through it) should be given up. When the talk was over, Piṅgiya had reached enlightenment16. A person who has paññā (wisdom) would not ask for anything else, however old and tired.

Life lasts one moment. The ancient texts say there are three kinds of death. Sammuti maraṇa (conventional17 death) is what everyone calls death, at the end of a life. Samuccheda maraṇa (final death) is the passing away of an arahant (a fully enlightened person), who is never born again. And khaṇika maraṇa (momentary18 death) is death at every moment. Life is a series of citta (moments of consciousness19), one after another. At this moment there is seeing. Seeing arises, sees, and dies, all in a flash. Then there is hearing, and it dies too. People say a life is long, but really life lasts for one moment of citta (consciousness) at a time. A person who understands this sees how pointless it is to cling to things that are gone before they can be held.

What is harder than swallowing a sword? A king in Magadha (a kingdom in India) had three wise councillors: Senaka, Āyura and Pukkusa. Senaka was the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be). A young man of the court fell in love with the queen and lay down sick with longing. The king took pity on him and said

that the queen might go to him for seven days. But the two of them fell in love and ran away to another country.

The king was so full of grief20 that he fell ill, and no doctor could cure him. Senaka knew that the sickness was in the king’s mind, and he thought of a cure. He arranged a show in which a man swallowed a sharp sword thirty-three inches long. The king asked the wise Āyura whether anything in the world was harder than that. Āyura answered that it is harder to say, “I shall give this away”. The king thought: I said I would give the queen, so I have done a hard thing. His grief grew a little lighter.

Then he asked Pukkusa whether anything was harder than saying one will give. Pukkusa answered that to make a promise and really let go of the thing is harder still. The king thought: I promised, and I did give her. His grief grew lighter still.

Then he asked Senaka whether anything was harder than giving. Senaka answered that the hardest thing of all is to give a gift and never regret it afterwards. The king thought: I gave the queen, and then I was sorry about it, and that was not right. What is the use of grieving over her? With that thought all his sorrow slid away like a drop of water off a lotus21 leaf, and he was well. The Buddha told this story to a monk22 who wanted to leave the Order because his former wife was tempting him. That monk had been the king. Āyura was Mahā-Moggallāna, Pukkusa was Sāriputta, and Senaka was the Buddha.

“This is harder to do than swallowing a sword of thirtythree inches long.” Saying one will give. Really giving. Giving and never regretting it.

Āyura the sword-swallower the king, sick with grief Senaka Pukkusa a sharp sword thirty-three inches long the three wise councillors “This is harder to do than swallowing a sword of thirtythree inches long.”

Regret. Regret after giving shows that there is still clinging to the thing given. But in truth there is nobody who owns it, and nobody who can keep it, because every rūpa (matter) and every nāma (mind) falls away23 the moment it has arisen. Wisdom that sees this can give without being sorry.

The angry moment. When someone is angry with another person, paññā (wisdom) can remember that the other person, in truth, is only citta (consciousness), cetasika (mental24 factors) and rūpa (matter), arising and falling away. That person will not be in this world for long. Nobody knows whether this meeting is the last one. A mind that remembers this becomes gentle, and mettā (loving-kindness25) can arise in place of the anger.

1. Which of these is nekkhamma (letting go) in daily life? (a) wanting to obtain still more pleasant things, never content with what one already has (b) not wishing to buy more clothing that only beautifies the body, because what one has is more than sufficient (c) savouring one more morsel because the food is so delicious, though one is not hungry (d) liking a warm bath for its pleasant feeling, even though the body does not need one 2. Chapter 5. Viriya (energy)

“I never grudge, O Prince, great sages who are seeking what is supreme and ready to pay them honour due with humble mind, I fall before their feet.”

Viriya (energy1) is effort. The ancient texts say it is the state of a courageous person. When viriya (energy) arises2, a person is not lazy or slack.

Viriya (energy) What it is striving What it does strengthens and supports How it shows itself not getting tired of the task an occasion for making an effort, or saṃvega (a sense of urgency3) What it needs Energy for good and energy for bad. Here is something most people never think about. The cetasika (mental factor4) viriya (energy) arises with almost every citta (consciousness5), good or bad. When there is attachment6 to something, energy is there, working for the attachment. Even a coward has viriya (energy), energy for cowardice. Even a lazy person has viriya (energy), energy that goes into being lazy again and again. So energy by itself is not a perfection7. The perfection of energy is effort for kusala (good). A question to ask: the viriya (energy) that arises now, is it kusala (good) or akusala (bad)? Most of the time it is likely to be working for lobha (attachment). Nobody makes the effort. When sati (mindfulness8) is aware of what appears at this moment, there is no “me” who makes an effort to be aware. The effort is the work of sammā-vāyāma (right effort), a cetasika (mental9 factor). Viriya (energy) is not weary of the task, even when understanding grows very slowly.

The Ten Perfections for Young Readers  ·  22

Page 22

Even giving needs energy. A person may have the good intention10 to give something away, and still not give it, because he is lazy. The thing is there, and the intention is there, but the viriya (energy) to carry it out is missing. The same is true of all the other perfections. Sometimes a person thinks that doing good is troublesome, or that he is too tired. At such moments akusala (bad states) have won. Life lasts one moment of citta (consciousness), so good should be done at once, not later.

Three pictures of energy. The Atthasālinī (The Expositor, an ancient commentary11) gives pictures of what viriya (energy) does.

The old house. An old house that is falling down is held up by new pillars. When viriya (energy) supports a person, good states do not fall away12 in him. Someone who is bored, lazy or sleepy is like a house that is falling down. The small army. A small army goes into battle and is pushed back. The king sends strong reinforcements, and the army wins. In the same way viriya (energy) does not let the good states retreat; it lifts them up. The ox in the marsh. A strong ox is set to pull a load out of a marsh. It presses the ground with its knees and does not let the load drop. In the same way viriya (energy) takes up the work of doing good and does not drop it.

the load

the ox: viriya (energy) the marsh presses the ground with its knees and does not let the load drop “the bullock, pressing the ground with its knees, were to carry the burden and would not allow it to drop on the ground”

The city of bandits and the city of peace. The Venerable Sāriputta gave this picture. There were two cities, a city of bandits and a city of peace. A general thought: so long as the city of bandits exists, the city of peace is not safe. So he put on his armour, went into the city of bandits, broke down its gate and its walls, filled in its moat and set fire to it. Then he went into the city of peace and sat down to a fine meal with his family. The city of bandits is sakkāya-diṭṭhi (personality belief, the wrong view13 that there is a self). The city of peace is nibbāna (the end of all troubles). The general is the person who develops the mind. Wrong view has to be destroyed first, and that takes courage.

the city of bandits the general the city of peace sakkāya-diṭṭhi (personality belief) the person who develops the mind nibbāna (the end of all troubles) the wrong view that there is a self “So long as the city of bandits exists the city of peace is not free from danger. I shall destroy the city of bandits.”

The hero. The Buddha was called vīra (a hero). The ancient texts say why: “He had perseverance and was therefore called a hero. He was valiant and was therefore called a hero. He caused others to persevere and was therefore called a hero.” Under the Bodhi tree, before he became the Buddha, he said that he would not move from his seat even if his skin, veins and bones dried up. That is viriya (energy) at its highest.

Four right efforts. The Buddha taught four sammā-ppadhāna (right efforts):

1. the effort to avoid akusala (bad states) that have not yet arisen 2. the effort to overcome akusala (bad states) that have arisen 3. the effort to develop kusala (good states) that have not yet arisen 4. the effort to keep the kusala (good states) that have arisen and bring them to completion Looking at oneself. The teachers of old said that a monk14 should examine himself three times a day: in the morning, in the daytime and in the evening. If he cannot do it three times, then twice. If he cannot do it twice, then once. But not to examine oneself at all is wrong. Nobody else can see a person’s akusala (bad states) as closely as that person can. Someone who examines himself honestly is “easy to speak to”. Someone who sees only other people’s faults is “difficult to speak to”. All of this depends on viriya (energy).

Energy is in the mind. The ancient texts say that viriya (energy) is always mental, never bodily. A monk who walks up and down to keep himself awake seems to be using bodily energy. In truth the walking happens because of viriya (energy), which is a cetasika (mental factor).

The man of eighty. The book tells of a man of about eighty who had listened to the teaching for many years. When he heard a radio talk about vipassanā (insight15), he wrote down the address of the Dhamma Study and Support Foundation and set out to go there to make a donation. He left his house at nine in the morning and arrived at two in the afternoon. He had no time for lunch. That is the viriya (energy) of an old man who went against his own comfort in order to do good.

Trying too hard. Some people want to see results16 quickly, so they strive with all their might. They get tired and have to stop. The result cannot be made to come sooner. Satipaṭṭhāna (mindfulness of realities17) is awareness18 of what naturally appears in daily life, and it cannot be hurried.

King Saṃvara. The Saṃvara Jātaka (birth story number 462) was told about a monk who had stopped trying. He had studied for five years, then gone to the forest and worked hard at his meditation19 for three months, and reached nothing. He decided that he could understand only the words, and went back to the Buddha. The Buddha told him that the highest fruit of the teaching cannot be reached by someone who is lazy, and that in the past he had been full of energy: although he had been the youngest of the hundred sons of the King of Vārāṇasī, he had become king.

King Saṃvara, the youngest of a hundred princes, was chosen as king by his brothers and the people because of his good qualities. His eldest brother, Prince Uposatha, asked him how this had come about. Saṃvara answered that he never grudged20 honour to the great sages21, but fell at their feet with a humble mind. Wise men taught him, and he liked to listen and had no envy22. He paid his soldiers what was due to them, and wise counsellors23 helped him, so that the city had plenty and merchants from other lands prospered24. When the people heard this, they saw that he was worthy to be king.

At the end the Buddha said: “Monk, long ago you followed the instruction, but why do you not now strive?” The monk became a sotāpanna (stream-enterer). He had been King Saṃvara. Sāriputta had been Prince Uposatha. The courtier25 who advised the king had been the Buddha himself.

Three occasions. The Buddha said that energy is to be put forth on three occasions: to prevent bad states that have not arisen, to bring about good states that have not arisen, and to endure26 bodily feelings that are painful and sharp. A person who makes an effort on these three occasions is called “strenuous27, wise and mindful so that he makes an end of dukkha”.

Chapter 6. Khanti (patience)

“He wanted to keep his purity of sīla and did not kill that monkey.”

Khanti (patience) is acceptance. The book says it has a wide meaning: patience is needed not only with what is unpleasant, but also with what is pleasant, so that lobha (attachment1) does not arise2 when something delightful appears.

Khanti (patience) What it is acceptance endures3 the desirable and the undesirable What it does How it shows itself tolerance4, not fighting back What it needs seeing things as they really are Two kinds of endurance. Someone may stay awake all night in order to get what he wants. That is endurance with lobha (attachment). The question is whether a person can put up with as much as that in order to develop kusala (good). That kind of endurance is the perfection5 of patience. “It is very hot.” With patience a person can stand heat or cold. That does not mean the weather changes. It means that because of hot or cold weather, akusala citta (bad consciousness6) does not arise. If the weather is liked, there is lobha (attachment); if it is disliked, there is dosa (aversion7); either way there is no patience. A person may say “It is very hot,” and akusala citta (bad consciousness) has probably already arisen. Patience with one’s surroundings, the weather, the place, the dhamma of each moment, is called adhivāsanā khanti (patience with one’s surroundings). The ancient texts say it is the highest tapa (burning away).

The Ten Perfections for Young Readers  ·  26

Page 26
Ten Perfections Baths. Some people love a warm bath, or a cold one (p. 16–30) p. 27

With people. People who do everything quickly should be patient with people who are slow. There is patience in speech too: before speaking, considering whether what is about to be said is of any use, and if it is not, keeping quiet. And there is no person who is patient. There are only sobhana cetasika (beautiful mental factors8) that have been developed.

What the commentary says of patience. The commentary9 praises patience in a long passage. Patience is “the unimpeded10 weapon of the good”, because it drives out anger, the enemy of all good qualities. It is “a stream of water extinguishing the fire of anger”, “an ocean on account of its depth”, and “a staircase ascending to the worlds of the gods and Brahmas”. Then it gives thoughts for the moment when someone does wrong to us:

If there were no wrong-doers11, how could the perfection of patience ever be accomplished? A wrongdoer is also a benefactor12. All beings13 are like my own children. Who becomes angry over the misdeeds14 of his own children? The deed15 by which wrong was done, and the one who did it, have at this very moment ceased16. With whom, then, should there be anger now? If the wrong-doer has good qualities, there is no reason to be angry with him. If he has none, he deserves compassion17. Anger is the only real enemy, and when one has patience one has no enemies.

The buffalo and the monkey. The Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was once born as a buffalo. A monkey came and dirtied him four times, on his shoulder, his forehead and his eyebrows. A yakkha (a spirit) told him to kill the monkey. The buffalo did not give in to anger. He wanted to keep his sīla (good conduct) pure, and he wanted to become a Buddha. He said that someone of wisdom, who forgives disrespect from the low, the middling18 and the high, obtains what he aspired19 to. Patience is to be developed towards everybody.

the monkey

the buffalo: the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) the yakkha (spirit) "Kill the monkey." He did not give in to anger. He wanted to keep his sīla (good conduct) pure.

“A yakkha advised him to kill that monkey, but the Bodhisatta did not give in to anger.”

Dhamma and Adhamma. In another life the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was a devaputta (son of a heavenly being) named Dhamma, and Devadatta was Adhamma. Dhamma came among people and taught the ten good deeds, and Adhamma taught the ten evil ones. One day their chariots20 met in mid-air, and each claimed the right of way. Adhamma said:

By iron gold is beaten, nor do we Gold used for beating iron ever see: If Wrong against Right shall win the fight today, Iron as beautiful as gold will be.

Dhamma answered that he would swallow all those evil words and give him the way. He gave way, with patience and loving-kindness21. And the earth opened and swallowed Adhamma. There is a lesson here for everyone who joins in blaming a wrongdoer again and again: at that moment the citta (consciousness) is akusala (bad), and the person is really on the side of Adhamma, not of Dhamma.

Dhamma: the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) Adhamma: Devadatta "gold" "iron"

Dhamma gave way. The earth opened and swallowed Adhamma.

the earth opened “One day their two chariots met in mid-air, and they each claimed the right of way.”

King Pukkusāti. King Pukkusāti ruled in Takkasilā and King Bimbisāra ruled in Rājagaha (two cities of ancient India). They had never met, but they became friends through the merchants who travelled between them. Pukkusāti sent Bimbisāra eight precious cloths. Bimbisāra wondered what he could send back that was finer. He was a sotāpanna (stream-enterer), and nothing gave him joy but the Tiratana (the Triple Gem: the Buddha, his teaching and his enlightened22 disciples23). So he had a sheet of gold made, and on it he had written the qualities of the Buddha, the ten perfections, the qualities of the Dhamma (the teaching) and the Saṅgha (the enlightened disciples), and the way to practise mindfulness24 of breathing. At the end he wrote that if his friend could really grasp this, he should become a monk25. He put the sheet in a box, that box in a golden box, and so on, box within box, and sent it off on his best elephant.

“This box was placed into another box of gold, and this golden box into a silver box, and each box was successively placed into another precious box”

Pukkusāti opened the boxes alone in his palace and began to read. When he read of the qualities of the Buddha, such joy arose that the hairs of his body stood on end, and he had to wait before he could read on. Then he practised mindfulness of breathing and reached jhāna (deep calm of mind). For a month nobody saw him but his page. The citizens complained that the king no longer looked after the city. The king asked himself: “Shall we maintain the Kingdom or shall we maintain the teachings?” He answered: the teachings. He cut off his hair with his sword, put on two yellow robes, took an earthenware26 bowl, and walked out of the palace. Nobody recognised him.

He walked on foot, as the Buddha had done. His feet, which had never walked on hot ground, blistered and bled. He ate the coarse27 food of the merchants he travelled with as if it were divine food. Because the letter said the Buddha had appeared at Rājagaha, he walked past Sāvatthī, where the Buddha really was, and on to Rājagaha. There a villager told him that the Buddha was at Sāvatthī. It was evening, so he took lodging in the workshop of a potter.

That morning the Buddha had seen him with his mind, and had thought: if I do not go, he will die tomorrow without reaching the third stage of enlightenment. So the Buddha walked forty-five leagues in half a day, came to the potter’s door and asked, as an ordinary monk, whether he might spend one night there. “Spacious, friend, is the potter’s dwelling,” said Pukkusāti; “stay, friend, according to your pleasure.” The Buddha spread grass on the dirty floor among the broken pots and sat down as if in his own fragrant chamber.

Later the Buddha asked him whose teaching he followed. “The recluse28 Gotama,” said Pukkusāti, and told him that he had never seen the Buddha and would not know him if he saw him. Then the Buddha taught him that the elements29 of earth, water, fire, wind, space and consciousness are not mine, not I, not myself. As he listened, Pukkusāti understood who was speaking. He bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet and asked forgiveness for having called the Teacher “friend”. The Buddha forgave him. Pukkusāti went out to look for a bowl and robe so that he could be ordained30, and a cow swerved and killed him. The Buddha said that he had become an anāgāmī (non-returner) and would reach nibbāna (the end of all troubles)

without returning to this world. Pukkusāti, who gave up a kingdom and walked all that way, must have had the utmost patience. And the Buddha, who walked the same road and slept on the floor of a potter’s shed, shows the patience to be developed with regard to seats and beds and everything in one’s surroundings.

The teaching of the Buddhas. The Ovāda-pāṭimokkha (the exhortation31 that sums up the teaching) begins with patience:

Khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā: patience, endurance, is the highest austerity32. Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadanti Buddhā: nibbāna is supreme, the Buddhas say. Na hi pabbajito parūpaghātī: he is not a recluse who harms another.

Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ: not doing any evil, kusalassa upasampadā: doing what is good, sacittapariyodapanaṃ: purifying33 one’s own mind, etaṃ Buddhāna sāsanaṃ: this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

A person who harms another, even a fly or a mosquito, cannot be called a recluse, because he lacks adhivāsanā khanti (patience with his surroundings).

The harm of impatience. The Buddha listed five things: the impatient person is not dear to many people; he is full of ill will34; much harm comes to him; he dies confused; and he is reborn35 in an unhappy place. An angry mind at the moment of death is a danger far worse than any danger in this world. Patience is needed above all to listen to the Dhamma, because the perfections take a very long time to develop.

The old monk and his sons. The Kassapamandiya Jātaka (birth story number 312) was told about an old monk. A young man had become a monk and soon an arahant (fully enlightened). When his mother died he persuaded his father and his younger brother to become monks too. One day the three were walking back to the Jeta Grove. The elder brother went ahead and told the novice36, the younger brother, to bring their father along slowly. The old man walked very slowly, and the boy, to hurry him, butted him in the back with his head. The old man was so angry that he turned round and walked back to where they had started, and this went on until it was dark. The next day the Buddha blamed the old monk, not the boy, and said that he had behaved the same way in a past life. In that life the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was an ascetic, and the old monk was his father. The son said to him: “Father, young boys are just like earthen vessels, they are broken in a moment. Once they are broken it is not possible to mend them. Young boys may be abusive37 or censure38 others, but old men should bear with them patiently.” And he spoke these lines:

Even wise men may quarrel, But quickly they can become closely united again. But fools part asunder like untempered39 clay, They cannot calm down their hate.

The old recluse trained himself from then on. But in his next life, the book says, he acted as he used to act. Defilements40 that have not been removed lie quiet and can arise at any time. The only cure is to develop paññā (wisdom) with patience, little by little.
